To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the weight-shifting capacity of patients with poststroke hemiparesis can be improved through intensive rehabilitation, that this improvement is associated with a decrease in the severity of motor deficits, and that it is not associated with an increase in the severity of sensory or cognitive deficits.

the use of a robotic device to provide weight shifting during rehabilitation after stroke can restore weight-shifting capacity and improve balance in patients who have had a stroke, and that these improvements are maintained after the device is removed.

1) the weight-shifting capacity of the hemiparetic leg was significantly reduced in poststroke patients and 2) the weight-shift capacity could be restored by using the body weight-supported treadmill training (BWSTT) in the postacute phase after stroke.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the restoration of weight-shifting ability and the ability to stand in patients with poststroke hemiparesis.
the restoration of weight-shifting (WS) capacity in postacute stroke survivors.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found a significant relationship between a change in the weight-shifting task and the ability to walk independently in the stroke population.

we found that the weight-shifting ability of patients with poststroke hemiparesis was improved by the use of the body-weight-supported treadmill training with partial weight-bearing (BWSTPWB), but not by the conventional gait training.

we have demonstrated the effectiveness of a novel, task-specific training approach for the restoration of weight shifting in stroke survivors, which is a fundamental component of balance and gait control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have developed a method to restore the weight-shifting capacity (WSC) of patients with postacute hemiparesis.
the use of virtual reality in stroke rehabilitation can be beneficial.
the use of the weight-shifting test (WST) in a rehabilitation context is a reliable and valid tool for assessing balance recovery in patients with poststroke hemiparesis.
